title: Brother Lawrence's letters
hookLine: a little lifting of the heart is enough
tomorrow: what did a mathematician keep sewn inside his coat?

lines: HOW LITTLE CAN A PRAYER BE?
cards: A thumbs-up. A two-letter text. A wave across a parking lot.
Small, and nobody thinks they're nothing; a friendship can run on them for weeks. So how little can a prayer be and still count? A whole hour on your knees?
Ten minutes with a book? Brother Lawrence got asked versions of that question by friends who wrote to him, and his answer was smaller than they expected.

teach.b: In his letters, put plainly, Lawrence says you don't have to be in church to be with God. You can make a little chapel of your heart, and step into it now and then, quietly, while you work. How long?
He says a little lifting of the heart is enough. A brief remembering of God. One act of inward worship.

teach.h: EVEN ON THE MARCH, SWORD IN HAND.
teach.b: Even, he writes, for a soldier on the march with a sword in hand: short prayers like that still count, and steady him. So the Christian answer here isn't about length at all. It's about how often you glance up.
Now a neighbor who knows this well.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Remember Allah with much remembrance." Muslims call that remembering dhikr.

A physical therapist who says bismillah, in the name of God, under his breath as a patient stands up, is doing a small version of it. Same instinct as Lawrence: God remembered in the middle of the task, briefly, often.
And one honest difference. Lawrence's lifting is wordless, a turn of the heart in his own way.
Dhikr is often carried by set words from the Qur'an and the Prophet's sayings, in Arabic, the same words across the world.
Two neighbors, both glancing up, each in their own words.

how: Some Christians follow Brother Lawrence's advice with brief turns to God through the day, sometimes on the hour; Muslims practice dhikr, the remembrance of God, often in short phrases from the Qur'an and the Prophet's sayings.

games.q: your aunt in the army says she has no time to pray on long training days. what do Lawrence's letters say about someone like her?
o: even on the march, sword in hand, a little lifting of the heart counts.
she should get up an hour earlier and pray before training starts.
soldiers are excused from prayer until they're off duty.
games.why: Lawrence wrote that short prayers made on the march still count, and steady a soldier rather than weaken her.

practice: Sit tall and lift your chin a little, the way you look up when someone you love walks into the room. Hold that small lift for one breath, then let it settle. Do it a few more times in the sit: lift, settle, lift.

wordCard.voice: Brother Lawrence's letters. Advice to friends from a kitchen: a chapel in the heart, and a prayer as small as a glance.

carryVoice: Carry this: a little lifting, which Lawrence says is enough even with a sword in your hand. See you tomorrow.
